summary:
Mission Design Lab is a web-based, card-driven game where players act as mission architects to design, launch, and operate a complete space mission. It addresses the challenge by translating complex systems engineering into an accessible 15-minute gameplay loop. Players select missions, spacecraft, and instruments while managing strict constraints like mass, power, budget, and data downlinks. During the flight phase, unexpected events test their engineering margins, teaching the core lesson that leftover capacity buys safety. 
This is important because mission trade-offs usually remain abstract for students. Our game grounds its phases directly in NASA's real Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1–4) and mission segments. The post-mission Trade-off Report explains exactly which design choices helped or hurt, transforming trial-and-error into a deep, intuitive understanding of real-world aerospace engineering.
details:
Mission Design Lab is an interactive, web-based card game where players act as mission architects to design, launch, and operate a complete space mission. Players select objectives and fill spacecraft slots with components (power, comms, instruments, launch vehicles). Live gauges track mass, power, cost, and data. Once the design passes a rigorous "Launch Check," the mission enters a flight phase where random event cards (e.g., solar storms, thruster glitches) test the engineering margins the player preserved. A final Trade-off Report explains exactly which design choices helped or hurt.

Benefits & Impact: Space mission trade-offs usually remain abstract for students. Our game makes systems engineering tangible, teaching the core lesson that leftover capacity (margins and reserves) buys safety during operations. It serves as a frictionless "mission-control classroom" accessible via any web browser.

Tools: React, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, Vitest. 100% client-side web application with original pixel art assets.

Creativity: We translated NASA’s rigorous Concept Maturity Level (CML) framework and systems engineering lifecycle into an accessible 15-minute gameplay loop. The core mechanic—where leftover build margins directly modify dice rolls during flight events—elegantly gamifies the engineering concept of "margins and reserves."

Factors Considered: We balanced educational fidelity with gameplay accessibility, ensuring the game models NASA's four mission segments (Launch, Space, Ground, User) and requirements verification without requiring advanced math. We also prioritized a client-only architecture for easy classroom deployment.
